newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish markets calm about Yeltsin health for now.
newsitem.headline: Polish markets calm about Yeltsin health for now.

text.p: Polish financial markets are watching for more news about the health of Russian President Boris Yeltsin, but on Monday analysts ruled out the possibility of a large impact in the near-term.
They said however, that if Yeltsin was forced to give up control of the Kremlin following his heart surgery in about two months time, the Warsaw bourse may react with a loss.

"If the operation didn't work out...it could have a negative impulse (on the bourse), otherwise there shouldn't be any sensation caused by Yeltsin's general health condition." Pawel Hominski, an analyst at Magnus brokerage told Reuters.

Analysts said this week's stock movements would be more closely linked to the possibility of an interest rate rise by the U.S. Federal Reserve on Tuesday than complications surrounding Yeltsin's planned bypass operation.
On Monday the Warsaw bourse's main WIG index rebounded 1.1 percent to 14,656.5 after a two-session dip.
"If foreigners are passive today it's more because they fear an interest rate rise in the United States tomorrow than because of Yeltsin's ill health." Mangus's Hominski said.

Analysts said the Polish debt market would probably have little reaction to Yeltsin's health problems unless foreign investors sell large amounts of T-bills and bonds from their portfolios, which they said was unlikely.

They expected the Polish zloty would weaken against the dollar if Yeltsin's operation fails to restore him as Russia's leader, as investors flock to the security of the U.S. currency during periods of international uncertainty.

"The Yeltsin issue will likely have little effect on the debt market, but the zloty could temporarily lose ground to the dollar if the U.S. currency gains on world markets," said Jacek Lech, deputy chief dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
Analysts said it was not likely that foreign investors would withdraw capital from Poland's, or other central European financial markets unless democratic structures in Russia crumble.

"Polish financial systems are strong and independent and I don't believe there will be an outflow of capital from Warsaw, Prague or Budapest as a result of this," said Andrzej Rzysko, treasurer at Societe Generale in Warsaw.
